planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring at the base of a fence, arbor, or open shrub it can twine through, in humus-rich soil with reliable moisture; it is most at home along a woodland edge rather than a hot open trellis.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil at a woodland edge or in dappled shade, giving the twining stems a fence, sapling, or trellis to climb since this species clasps rather than clings. The whole plant, including the paired leaves that fuse into a cup below the flower cluster, is noticeably downy to the touch, which is the trait behind both its scientific and common names and a quick way to tell it apart from smoother-leaved native honeysuckle vines. Terminal whorls of yellow-orange tubular flowers open in early summer and are followed by clustered orange-red berries that ripen through fall and are taken by woodland birds. It spreads modestly by twining rather than rooting or seeding aggressively, making it a well-mannered choice compared to the invasive Japanese honeysuckle it is sometimes confused with at a glance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in fall to take advantage of the Mediterranean-climate rainy season, siting them at the base of an oak, fence, or trellis in fast-draining soil; established plants need little to no summer irrigation.

directions: Plant in fast-draining soil in dappled shade to partial sun, where this Pacific Coast native scrambles through chaparral shrubs and oak woodland edges from British Columbia to central California; give it a fence, shrub, or trellis to twine through since it climbs by wrapping rather than clinging. Whorled clusters of pink to purplish-pink tubular flowers open in late spring atop the fused, disc-like uppermost leaf pairs typical of native honeysuckle vines, followed by translucent red berries that ripen through summer. Once established it tolerates the dry summers of its native range with little supplemental water, making it a useful low-input vine for western gardens that mimic natural woodland-edge conditions. It is not aggressive and stays well-behaved compared to non-native honeysuckle vines that can overrun a fence or hedge.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in cool, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; this species is adapted to the deep shade and consistent moisture of northern hardwood forests and struggles in hot, exposed sites.

directions: Plant in cool, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beneath an established tree canopy, where this upright understory shrub grows naturally across northeastern forests from the Maritimes and Great Lakes south through the Appalachians. It is among the earliest native honeysuckles to flower, opening pale yellow, funnel-shaped blooms in loose pairs on slender stalks while the surrounding canopy is still leafing out, well ahead of most other woodland shrubs. Paired, bright red berries follow in early summer and are stripped quickly by thrushes and other songbirds, so the display is often brief. Unlike the twining honeysuckle vines, this is a freestanding shrub that needs no trellis and fits naturally into a shaded native understory planting alongside ferns and spring ephemerals.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this montane native is adapted to cold winters and a short, cool growing season and does poorly in hot, humid climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking the coniferous mountain forests of the Rockies and Intermountain West where this compact shrub grows at mid to high elevation. In spring it bears small paired flowers in pale yellow shading to pink, followed by red berries that are fused at the base into a distinctive double-lobed fruit and are readily eaten by grouse and songbirds. It forms a tidy, rounded understory shrub that needs no staking or support, making it a fitting companion for other cold-hardy montane natives in a shaded rock garden or woodland border. Give it good drainage and cool root conditions, since it is far less tolerant of summer heat and humidity than eastern honeysuckle species.
